brief: Zero Hedge aggregates JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and Nomura positioning desks after a week in which the S&P fell seven straight sessions, the Nasdaq 100 lost 10.4% and the SOX shed 17%. Hedge funds had their worst 5-day P&L since April 2025 (JPMorgan: down >3%; Goldman fundamental L/S: down 1.2-1.6% Friday), driven by beta long exposure rather than bad stock-picking, since alpha stayed flat to positive. Net leverage fell to multi-year lows (Goldman fundamental L/S net at the 1st percentile) while gross leverage rose to a 98th-percentile high, because funds added shorts instead of cutting exposure. Historically this magnitude of hedge-fund de-risking has preceded a bounce, and JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Goldman's macro desk and Mike Wilson all called for one, but it hasn't arrived, because hedge funds are no longer the marginal seller: CTAs, asset managers, long-onlys and retail (which added $59bn to equity funds) haven't capitulated. The piece argues the 2018 analog, a late-November bounce followed by a harder December selloff, requires the rest of the market plus a Fed pivot to confirm it, and bets that script still has room to run since the Fed is still hiking.
